question_bank.stem: How does the instructor contrast generative modeling with ordinary classification?

options.text: Generative models learn the data distribution rather than just assigning class labels.
Generative models remove the data distribution and keep only class labels.
Generative models classify existing examples rather than producing new samples.
Generative models replace probability modeling with fixed lookup tables.

question_bank.explanation: The core contrast is that discriminative models classify, while generative models learn a data distribution from which samples can be created.

distractor_rationales.C: Describes discriminative classification rather than generation.
distractor_rationales.D: Replaces the probabilistic framing with an unsupported lookup-table idea.

frame_evidence.description: Slide introduces generative modeling use cases before contrasting distribution learning with classification.

question_bank.stem: Which set of examples best matches the generative-modeling use cases discussed at the start of the section?

options.text: Image and video generation, captioning, code generation, and inpainting.
Image labeling, binary classification, cost plotting, and red teaming.
Gradient masking, input filtering, data review, and output sanitization.
Patch printing, detector scoring, black-box querying, and transfer attacks.

question_bank.explanation: The instructor solicits use cases and mentions image/video generation, captioning, code generation, super-resolution, and inpainting.

distractor_rationales.B: Mixes classification and GAN diagnostics rather than generative use cases.
distractor_rationales.C: Lists adversarial defenses rather than content generation tasks.
distractor_rationales.D: Lists adversarial patch concepts rather than generative-model applications.

frame_evidence.description: Instructor asks for examples of generative modeling while the section slide is visible.

question_bank.stem: Why does the instructor say large datasets help a smaller generative model learn useful regularities?

options.text: The model has pressure to learn salient patterns instead of memorizing the dataset.
The model has pressure to store each image as a separate output label.
The model has pressure to discard probability and optimize classification accuracy.
The model has pressure to use adversarial triggers as training labels.

question_bank.explanation: The self-supervised intuition is that a model smaller than the dataset must learn patterns rather than memorize every example.

distractor_rationales.B: Describes memorization, which the instructor says the setup avoids.
distractor_rationales.D: Brings in backdoor triggers from the previous section.

frame_evidence.description: Instructor explains the self-supervised intuition after listing generative use cases.

question_bank.stem: What is the distribution-matching endpoint for a trained generative model in the lecture?

options.text: The generated distribution aligns with the real-world data distribution.
The generated distribution avoids the real-world data distribution.
The generated distribution becomes a single most likely training example.
The generated distribution becomes the classifier decision boundary.

question_bank.explanation: Training is considered successful when generated samples follow the real data distribution.

distractor_rationales.C: Confuses distribution matching with mode collapse or memorization.
distractor_rationales.D: Confuses generative sampling with a classifier boundary.

source_ref.evidence_span: What you want ultimately is that the red distribution is in line

frame_evidence.description: Slide plots real and generated distributions as the instructor describes alignment.
